Back in the old DOS days, there were a ton of games where shareware was the name of the game for us poor kids. Raptor was one such title, and perhaps the most relevant and pertinent title that would introduce me to the sh'mup genre. Only Bravo Sector was present in the shareware version, and I played for hours and hours looping through this on my dad's old 386.

30 some years later, color me surprised when Raptor, of all things, shows up on Steam. While it's nothing fancy and is little more than a prepacked DOSBOX emulation -- something those of us who cared enough likely dredged up from the abandonware sites years ago -- the fundamental convenience of having it integrated smoothly into Steam for a whopping $1 on sale, and subsequently throwing some change back to Apogee after all these years. It's really cool seeing someone go through the effort of trying to preserve these types of games as, though aged, they really harken back to how far computing has come.

The gameplay feels as you'd expect from a DOS game, but it doesn't play clunky and, unlike some old DOS titles which really struggle to map into the modern age, the game is definitely still enjoyable. There are still plenty of challenging quips playing on Veteran mode, and Elite certainly will keep any genre vet on their toes. Spritework remains crisp and delivers satisfactory explosions and visual mayhem as you shred everything in sight.  

I've only yet completed Bravo Sector, so I'm looking forward to actually stepping in and playing the other two sectors gated behind childhood imagination and poverty. What an awesome effort by Apogee (despite the transition of studio owners) to keep their work alive.

Raptor: Call of the Shadows (1994 Classic Edition) remains one of the most defining PC shoot-’em-ups of its era, and revisiting it today reveals just how cleverly constructed it always was. At first glance, it looks like a straightforward vertical-scrolling arcade shooter: you fly a heavily armed fighter jet, tear through waves of enemies, dodge incoming fire, and try to survive increasingly punishing missions. But beneath that simple exterior is a surprisingly strategic backbone built on resource management, weapon customization, and a satisfying rhythm of earning money through destruction and reinvesting it into better gear. That upgrade-focused loop gives the game a rewarding sense of progression rarely found in shooters of the time, making each run feel like a step toward crafting the deadliest aircraft imaginable.

The game’s structure is split into three campaigns, each consisting of nine missions that escalate in intensity. Every wave brings a barrage of air enemies, fortified ground defenses, and massive boss encounters that test reflexes and planning. What elevates the experience is the way Raptor blends pure arcade action with thoughtful preparation. Destroying enemies showers you with cash, and between missions you can spend those earnings on new weapons, shields, or experimental upgrades. Because weapons stack rather than replace each other, your ship becomes an increasingly elaborate death machine—if you’re careful with where you invest. That risk-reward economy, especially when selling equipment returns only half its value, forces you to think ahead. Every purchase matters, and it adds a layer of tension that makes victory feel earned rather than handed to you.

Combat is fast, crunchy, and satisfying. The weapon selection ranges from spread shots and tracking turrets to beam lasers and devastating bombs that clear entire screens. Each tool feels distinct, and discovering combinations that suit your playstyle becomes one of the game’s lasting joys. The steady growth from a lightly armed starter ship to a fully outfitted powerhouse is tangible in both visuals and gameplay—your screen-clearing volleys become a kind of reward for all the risks taken earlier. And yet, despite the power fantasy, Raptor never stops being challenging. Enemy formations grow more aggressive, ground installations fire from awkward angles, and bosses flood the screen with projectiles. It’s a difficulty curve that preserves the feel of classic arcade design while rewarding players who master the game’s patterns and pacing.

Raptor also remains striking in its presentation. Its crisp VGA pixel art still carries a charm that modern retro shooters try to emulate. Backgrounds shift from industrial complexes to dense forests, icy landscapes, cities under siege, and alien ruins, each with a strong sense of atmosphere. Enemies explode in vivid fragments, and the constant thrum of lasers, gunfire, and heavy impacts gives the game a brute, crunchy quality fitting its industrial sci-fi tone. The soundtrack is unmistakably 90s—energetic, looping, and unapologetically MIDI—but it complements the gameplay with a nostalgic energy that modern remasters wisely preserve rather than replace.

Though the game’s age is visible in places, these quirks contribute to its enduring personality. Some weapon balancing can feel uneven, and a few missions demand pattern memorization that may frustrate newcomers, but these elements represent an era of design built on challenge and mastery. The restrictive economy, the need to survive long enough to upgrade, and the precision required to get through later missions all reflect an uncompromising philosophy that still feels refreshing today. Far from being a simple relic, Raptor showcases how a tight design philosophy can outlast technological generations.

Ultimately, Raptor: Call of the Shadows succeeds because it merges adrenaline-fueled arcade action with the long-term satisfaction of building and perfecting your fighter. It stands as both a preserved slice of 90s PC gaming history and a genuinely enjoyable shooter in its own right. For long-time fans, the Classic Edition is a faithful return to a beloved title. For newcomers, it’s a chance to experience one of the genre’s most influential works—a game that continues to soar despite the decades behind it.

Raptor: Call of Shadows is a cult classic shoot 'em up from the late DOS days. It's a quality "Euro shmup" even though it was developed in the USA, it just has a lot of traits of what people have posthumously called Euro shmups, like a fairly deep upgrade system. In fact, like most Euro shumps with upgrade systems, knowing what to upgrade and when is key to getting through the game. There's a nice risk/reward system in place as you can avoid enemies fairly well, but the more enemies you shoot the more money you make for the shop in-between levels, and you can replenish your health with that money. It's a good game if you like the type with nice music.

There have been a lot of commercially versions released on PC over the years, here's the breakdown:

1994 - Original DOS version
2010 - GOG version, which is the 1994 original via DOSBox (no longer for sale)
2014 - Steam version, same as above
2015 - A different Steam version called "2015 edition" which has achievements and texture smoothing
2018 - Zoom Platform version, same as the 2010 GOG and original 2014 Steam versions

It's nice to have achievements in the 2015 version, but the texture smoothing is ugly (but optional) and it only plays at 24fps. It also has a slightly remastered soundtrack, which I think is okay. The DOSBox version has a lot of nice options in DOSBox itself, like 5x upscaling, aspect ratio lock, double buffering, and more. But it controls a little more sluggishly than the 2015 version. Considering they both go on sale for 50 cents each, get 'em both!

I am extremely good at bullet hell games. That being said: 

1. The screen/playzone should be bigger. You barely have any space to dodge, and the controls are not great, very finicky and you move very fast, hard to make small adjustments. Not to mention, you realistically have about 0.5 seconds to kill an enemy, or it just flies off screen. You earn money by killing enemies. You need money to get the stronger weapons or else you are literally useless and can't hurt anything. 

2. The loot enemies drop is hilariously worthless. Some enemies drop extra money... $50... to put it in perspective to purchase a "good weapon" it costs around $700,000. You would need to collect 14 thousand of these LOL. They are literally not even worth picking up. The main way you earn money is by picking up weapons you already have. 

3. The game punishes you for close calls, and comebacks are punitive. As in, let's say you almost die, but not quite. Well, remember that weapon you spent the entire game saving for, that you absolutely cannot hurt anyone without at the later stages? If your energy runs low, your weapons just disappear. You don't get them back at the end of the level, there is no way to recover them. Even if you somehow beat the odds and clear the level with 1 hp left, there's no point. You would be insane to not load your previous save because you're useless and can't deal damage anymore. 

4. Bosses have about a 1 second window to attack them. 

5. There is some enemy in the first wave of the outer regions that 100-0'd me in a single shot from off screen. It was a laser that seems to travel the screen instantly. Never had a chance to dodge, just blown up instantly. 

6. I could honestly forgive all of that... but you have to go to the 21st page of the manual to find out what the controls are. LOL. TWENTY ONE PAGES later, you can find out how to play the game. What on earth were they thinking?????

Easily the best shmup I have played, and I've played dozens. A close second would be Tyrian, which is objectively superior in some respects - such as in having more customization, upgrades, secret levels, et cetera - but as a complete package I believe the Raptor rules supreme. 

It's not that it's flawless, far from it. If you decide to dispassionately analyse it in a mechanical sense and deconstruct it, you will be able to tear it to pieces. I am not saying this is the most mechanically brilliant shmup, I'm not trying to make that sort of argument at all. 

What I *am* saying, is that it's the best shmup *experience* I've ever had. If you allow the game to take you on the a journey and get immersed in it, it is truly excellent, because it simply has a certain unique atmosphere and feeling to it. All the aspects work together - the aesthetics, the soundtrack, the sound effects, the way it plays, ... 

This isn't a game about numbers, it's not for competitive players, nor is it for those looking for some sort of hardcore bullet hell challenge - it's nothing of the sort. If I am to be perfectly honest, it's a deeply irrational game. It's ultimately about the way it *feels*. From the very moment you enter the hangar and the brooding music starts playing, you have to allow it to get under your skin. And then you will either fall in love with it, as many have, or hate it, because it's not for you. But if you approach it analytically, you are bound to not understand the Raptor at all and to reach some very wrong conclusions. To hyperfocus on its individual mechanics is wholly misguided. You just have to feel it and either it will resonate with you or it won't. 

With that said... if you do want to give it a go, please go into the setup.exe via the provided DOSbox launcher and set Sound Canvas as your music card and Sound Blaster as your SFX card. That is the highest quality sound you can get in both cases. 

Lastly... I highly recommend this game if you love shmups as a concept, but you despise traditional shmup mechanics such as one hit death or crazy bullet hell patterns. The Raptor bends or breaks many rules of the genre and isn't designed to punish you. It's not one of those old coin-up shmups, which exist solely to milk as much money from you as possible. It *will* still kill you very quickly if you let your guard down or get sloppy - it's not a shmup designed for games journalists, if that's you're worried about. But it does only seeks to challenge you insofar the challenge makes for a good time. It's not hard just to flex at you and to show you how difficult it can be while remaining *technically* fair by being beatable. The Raptor isn't one of those shmups. 

If you truly want to make the game hard, you have to impose artificial restrictions on yourself, such as by not buying certain weapons or not buying extra shields. Which is really fun actually. But if you do utilise all the tools made available to you, it's just a good time, not something, where you'll be bashing your head against a wall, trying to memorise boss patterns and train muscle memory just to execute the perfect dance in a sea of projectiles. 

Honestly, overall difficulty would be one of my criticisms. Once you figure the game out, it becomes fairly easy to you and you can create further challenge only by artificial means. But that only concerns people like me, who have played the Raptor many times since childhood. If you're completely new to this, you'll have a lot of fun figuring things out and learning how it all works. 

TL;DR: If you love shmups as a concept, but dislike one-hit-death bullet-hell shmups, this may be the game for you. If you love games that prioritise excellent atmosphere and immersion over meticulously crafted mechanics, this may also be for you.

Típico Shmup da era MS-DOS dos anos 90 quando a Apogee era a rainha do Shareware (ela possui tb Major Stryker e o Stargunner). Aqui a mecânica é a mesma usada mais tarde em Stargunner, selecione uma missão, tente sobreviver se esquivando dos tiros dos inimigos e mate-os se possível, nesse meio tempo recolha bônus em forma de dinheiro que poderá usar na lojinha entre missões para equipar sua nave com armas mais poderosas. As naves inimigas se movimentam rápido pela tela e em zigue-zague, melhor não permanecer na frente delas, algumas podem acabar com vc numa única rajada. Existem pelo menos 3 remakes desse game para Windows, nenhum vale a pena pois as mudanças são pequenas e o último é bugado. Recomendo Raptor para veteranos daqueles dias, quando precisávamos configurar o endereço da placa de som antes de iniciar o jogo, entretanto tem apelo zero para os mais novos, tirando o fator nostalgia, não há motivo para escolher Raptor com tanta coisa moderna infinitamente melhor aqui mesmo no Steam.

Nostalgia shmup done right. Perfected, even. 

This 1994 gem is a great nostalgia trip for everyone who has played this game at least once in their lives (if not, then it is a great starting point for the shmup genre), blasting you all the way back to the glorious days of 90s DOS gaming with crisp MIDI soundtrack.

As a side note, this game might have performance issues on lower end systems, since it is [b]emulated[/b] rather than natively ran.
